title: Start Cholesterol Tests at 17, Not 40: Dr. Devi Shetty's Warning to Indians
excerpt: India's leading cardiac surgeon calls for aggressive early screening as data shows nearly 9 in 10 Indian adults have abnormal cholesterol levels, with heart disease striking a decade earlier than in Western populations.
body:
• Dr. Devi Prasad Shetty, founder of Narayana Health, recommends cholesterol screening for all Indians starting at age 17, citing new Cardiology Society of India guidelines.
  • Men aged 35-40 should undergo routine cardiac CT scans, while those with family history of heart disease should begin checkups at 30.
  • South Asians face disproportionately higher cardiovascular risk, often developing heart disease a decade earlier than Western populations.
  • A normal cardiac CT scan may not need to be repeated for seven to ten years, making early screening a cost-effective preventive measure.

Dr. Devi Prasad Shetty, one of India's most prominent cardiac surgeons and founder of Narayana Health, has issued a renewed call for early and routine cholesterol screening across all age groups, warning that heart disease among Indians is striking younger and harder than global averages suggest.

Speaking in Bengaluru, Dr. Shetty said every Indian should undergo a cholesterol blood test by the age of 17 — a recommendation backed by updated guidelines from the Cardiology Society of India. The push comes as cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death in India, with a growing share of cases appearing in patients under 40.

Why Indians Face Higher Risk

The data is sobering. Research from the South Asian Heart Center shows that South Asians develop coronary artery disease at rates three to four times higher than other ethnic groups. Contributing factors include genetic predisposition to high Lipoprotein(a) levels, visceral fat distribution, insulin resistance, and dietary patterns heavy in refined carbohydrates.

A massive ICMR study published in August 2026 found that nearly 87 percent of Indian adults have at least one form of dyslipidemia — abnormal cholesterol or triglyceride levels. The study reinforced what cardiologists like Dr. Shetty have been arguing for years: heart disease in India is not a problem of old age but of biology and lifestyle compounding from the teenage years onward.

"Anyone with a family history of heart disease must go for a check-up at the age of 30."

— Dr. Devi Prasad Shetty, Founder and Chairman, Narayana Health

The Screening Protocol

Dr. Shetty laid out a tiered approach to cardiac screening. At age 17, a simple blood test can flag elevated LDL cholesterol and other lipid abnormalities early enough for lifestyle intervention — dietary changes, exercise, and monitoring — before the condition progresses silently.

For men between 35 and 40, he recommended a cardiac CT scan, which can detect calcium buildup in coronary arteries years before symptoms appear. If the scan comes back normal, Dr. Shetty noted, it may not need to be repeated for seven to ten years, making it a practical and cost-effective tool.

People with diabetes, he emphasized, should undergo cardiac evaluation even earlier, given the accelerated vascular damage associated with the condition. He also stressed that basic heart checkups, including tests that can be completed within an hour, should be done annually.

The Fitness Paradox

Addressing a pattern that has alarmed physicians — sudden cardiac deaths during exercise — Dr. Shetty cautioned against equating physical fitness with cardiac health. He noted that many people wrongly assume they are healthy simply because they feel fit, while underlying conditions like congenital heart defects or undetected plaque buildup go undiagnosed.

With adventure and endurance sports growing in popularity among young Indians, Dr. Shetty said cardiac screening is essential even for teenagers participating in extreme sports. The incidents of cardiac arrest during marathons, gym workouts, and cricket matches have put the spotlight on a gap between perceived health and actual cardiac risk.

The Carbohydrate Factor

In earlier interviews, Dr. Shetty has also challenged the conventional focus on dietary fats, arguing that carbohydrates — rice, chapati, sugar, and sweets — are the primary drivers of metabolic dysfunction in Indian populations. "Don't blame the oil, but sweets, sugar, rice, chapati. Carbohydrates are the villain," he told News18 in a previous interaction, advocating for daily walking, yoga, and reduced carbohydrate intake as frontline defenses.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans and NRIs, the message carries particular weight. The South Asian Heart Center recommends comprehensive cardiovascular screening for all South Asian adults over 18, including advanced markers like Apo B and Lipoprotein(a) that standard lipid panels often miss. With South Asians making up one of the fastest-growing demographic groups in the United States, the gap between standard screening protocols and population-specific risk remains a persistent public health blind spot.

Dr. Shetty's recommendations align with a growing consensus among cardiologists that the Indian population requires earlier, more aggressive screening than current Western guidelines prescribe. For families with a history of heart disease, the window for intervention begins not at middle age, but in the late teens.
